title.analysis: Authentic title "You Can't Afford a House. Good." is a short contrarian/permission frame: the first sentence states a negative, the second ("Good.") reverses it and promises a reframe of a housing-affordability fear. Against the frozen same-channel 10-peer cohort the video is 1.96499x (TYPICAL); against the 5-peer sensitivity cohort 2.28387x (STRONG), so the tier is unstable. Title promises reassurance; the script is a rent-versus-buy polemic ("buying is a trap"), so the "Good." is delivered as reframing, not comfort. Association only.

script.stored_text_completeness: All 18486 canonical characters read sequentially in full in 2 bounded ranges; auto-generated untimed text; stored ending is complete ("Now go use it."); many fillers ("Um"); ASR slips ("Schroinger's wealth", "can't rate at 2 a.m.", "$1.2 2 million", "monthtomonth", "20inut drive"); audio, timed delivery and editing unverified.
script.opening_words: Your coworker just bought a house. Um, you know this because they won't stop talking about it. They show you pictures of their new kitchen during lunch break, like it's their firstborn child, the granite countertops, the open floor plan, the half-finished base
script.ending_words: ize they're losing until they're 50 and still making payments on a house that owns them more than they own it. Real wealth is being able to say no to things that look like opportunities but calculate out as traps. You just learned how to say no. Now go use it.
script.analysis: Full 18486 canonical characters read. A rent-versus-buy polemic: scripted-character hook (smug coworker), thesis "renting is not throwing money away, buying is a trap", mortgage-cost breakdown, $2,000/month investing counterfactual ($2.4M vs $970K house), the "Johnsons" household budget, thesis-restating rhetoric (HELOC, 30-year loans, wealth extraction), a $50,000 down-payment-invested plus $500/month calculation, flexibility argument, and a "run your own numbers" spreadsheet homework close. Strong narrative engine (second-person, concrete dollar figures) but the arithmetic is selectively framed: the same video uses $2,000, $500 and then $4,000 monthly gaps; the 5-year Johnsons interest is understated by $39,000; and equity, appreciation and tax benefits are excluded from the owner side while the renter side assumes perfect discipline and 7-10% returns. No sources are named in the script.
beat_map: Hook: smug coworker just bought a house; "What's wrong with me?" pivot.
Thesis: "renting is throwing money away" is a lie; "we're going to mathematically destroy that lie."
Mortgage breakdown: $400K house, $350K at 7%, $2,330 payment, year-1 interest vs principal.
Add-ons: tax, insurance, maintenance, PMI; $3,500-4,000 "reality"; "less than 10% efficiency" car analogy.
Opportunity cost: renter invests $2,000/month at 7% = $2.4M vs $970K house; the "forced savings" caveat.
Who profits from advice: agents, brokers, banks; parents' 1987 house anecdote.
The Johnsons: $180K income, itemised $8,250 budget, $2,750 left, "feel broke".
Equity-is-not-real-money argument; $60K equity vs $80K interest; job-loss "eight weeks" scenario.
Rebuttals: "my house doubled" (so did everything), HELOC as new debt.
30-year mortgage "proof" houses are unaffordable; "wealth extraction machine".
Prescription: rent at 25% of take-home, invest the difference, ask owners to run real numbers.
Plan: $50K in index fund = $872K; $500/month = $1.1M; total near $2M vs $275K house profit ("factor of seven").
Psychology and flexibility: sitcom norms, move for jobs, downsize, "liquidity is freedom".
Opportunity cost narrative: "fossilized" money; uncle who bought in 1995; "real flex is having options".
Homework: spreadsheet rent-plus-invest versus owning, run 10 and 20 years.
Close: "Real wealth is being able to say no to things that look like opportunities but calculate out as traps."

claim_audit.claim: Say you buy a $400,000 house with a $350,000 mortgage at 7% interest over 30 years. Your monthly payment is roughly $2,330.
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
Say you buy a $400,000
house with a $350,000
mortgage at 7% interest over 30 years.
Your monthly payment is roughly $2,330.
claim_audit.assessment: [INDEPENDENT_CALCULATION_VERIFIED] $350,000 at 7%/12 over 360 months = $2,328.56 per month. [PRIMARY_SOURCE_DIRECTLY_INSPECTED] FRED MORTGAGE30US weekly Freddie Mac rate was 6.16% (2026-01-08), 6.06% (01-15), 6.09% (01-22), so the 7% assumption is about 0.9 points above the rate prevailing at upload and overstates payment and interest. $50,000 down on $400,000 is 12.5%.
claim_audit.date_scope: Video publication context 2026-01-23; source dates and access limitations in companion receipts

claim_audit.claim: In year 1, you're paying about $2,000 per month in interest. only $330 is going toward the principal
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
In
year 1, you're paying about $2,000 per
month in interest. only $330 is going
toward the principal
claim_audit.assessment: [INDEPENDENT_CALCULATION_VERIFIED] Month-1 interest $2,041.67 and principal $286.89 (not $330); year-1 interest $24,387 (video: $24,000, verified); year-1 principal is about $3,570 in total. Principal rises each month, so $330 is closer to month 3. Later "$4,000 total, $330 builds equity" mixes a month-1 figure with a rounded total.
claim_audit.date_scope: Video publication context 2026-01-23; source dates and access limitations in companion receipts

claim_audit.claim: Property taxes on a $400,000 house average around $4,000 to $6,000 per year, depending on your state.
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:

claim_audit.assessment: [ANALYST_RECALL_NOT_REVERIFIED] Implies 1.0-1.5% of value; recalled national effective rates are nearer 0.9-1.1%, with wide state spread. Insurance $150-300 and PMI $200-300 monthly also recall and not inspected. Not checked against Census ACS or ICE/Freddie data.
claim_audit.date_scope: Video publication context 2026-01-23; source dates and access limitations in companion receipts

claim_audit.claim: Let's add it up. Um, your $2,330 mortgage payment just became a $3,500 to $4,000 per month reality
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
Let's add it up. Um, your
$2,330
mortgage payment just became a $3,500
to $4,000 per month reality
claim_audit.assessment: [INDEPENDENT_CALCULATION_VERIFIED] $2,329 + tax $333-500 + insurance $150-300 + maintenance $333 (+ PMI $200-300) = $3,145-$3,762 without PMI, up to about $4,060 with it; the stated $3,500-4,000 is the upper range. The follow-on "$3,670 thrown away" subtracts $330 from a rounded $4,000. The frame treats all of interest, tax, insurance and repairs as pure loss, so the comparison with rent that also pays a landlord margin, tax and insurance is one-sided; principal ($330) is counted but appreciation is not.
claim_audit.date_scope: Video publication context 2026-01-23; source dates and access limitations in companion receipts

claim_audit.claim: that $2,000 per month becomes roughly $2.4 million. Meanwhile, person B's $400,000 house, assuming 3% annual appreciation, is worth about $970,000.
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
that $2,000 per month becomes

claim_audit.assessment: [INDEPENDENT_CALCULATION_VERIFIED] $2,000/month at 7%/12 for 30 years = $2,439,942; $400,000 at 3% for 30 years = $970,905; total interest on $350,000 at 7% = $488,281 ("over $480,000", verified). 7% is called conservative though it is a nominal pre-tax, no-fee, no-sequence-risk return; the comparison also assumes the renter pays $2,000 rent that never rises.

claim_audit.claim: after spending $480,000 in interest plus $150,000 in maintenance. Person A has $2.4 million in liquid investments.
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
after spending $480,000

maintenance. Person A has $2.4 million

claim_audit.assessment: [INDEPENDENT_CALCULATION_VERIFIED] 1% of a fixed $400,000 for 30 years is $120,000; 1% of a house appreciating 3% a year is $190,000. $150,000 matches neither. The $2.4M versus $970,000 (house, no sale costs) gap comes mostly from assuming a renter invests the entire $2,000 gap every month at 7% for 30 years, which the script concedes is the critical assumption.

a dual

claim_audit.claim: The Johnson's have maybe $60,000 in equity after 5 years of payments. That sounds impressive until you realize they paid $80,000 in interest to get it.
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
The Johnson's have maybe $60,000 in
equity after 5 years of payments. That
sounds impressive until you realize they
paid $80,000 in interest to get it.
claim_audit.assessment: [INDEPENDENT_CALCULATION_VERIFIED] Contradicted: 5-year interest on $350,000 at 7% is $119,174 (not $80,000); principal repaid $20,539, so equity is $70,539 with no appreciation or $134,249 with 3% appreciation (down payment $50,000 included). "Negative return" ignores appreciation and the rent avoided; the correct comparison needs both.
claim_audit.date_scope: Video publication context 2026-01-23; source dates and access limitations in companion receipts

claim_audit.claim: Miss three payments and the bank doesn't care about your equity. They take the house, keep everything you paid
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
Miss three payments
and the bank doesn't care about your
equity. They take the house, keep
everything you paid
claim_audit.assessment: [ANALYST_RECALL_NOT_REVERIFIED] US servicing rules recalled to bar a first foreclosure filing until 120 days delinquent and foreclosure sale proceeds exceeding the debt go to the owner, so "three payments" and "keep everything" overstate; not rechecked against CFPB 12 CFR 1024.41 or state law. The "eight weeks" runway for the Johnsons is a hypothetical with $2,750 of monthly slack and no stated emergency fund.
claim_audit.date_scope: Video publication context 2026-01-23; source dates and access limitations in companion receipts

claim_audit.claim: You take that $50,000 you didn't dump into a down payment. You invest it in a boring S&P 500 index fund. Historically, that returns about 10% annually. In 30 years, without adding another dollar, that $50,000 could grow to around $872,000.
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
You take

500 index fund. Historically, that
returns about 10% annually. In 30 years,
without adding another dollar, that

claim_audit.assessment: [INDEPENDENT_CALCULATION_VERIFIED] $50,000 x 1.10^30 = $872,470 (verified). [ANALYST_RECALL_NOT_REVERIFIED] About 10% is a recalled long-run nominal total-return figure (roughly 7% real); no series inspected here. claim_audit.claim: Say you're saving $500 a month by renting instead of owning. When you factor in maintenance, insurance, property taxes, and PMI, that's $6,000 a year. You invest that, too. After 30 years, that stream of investments turns into an additional $1.1 million.
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
Say you're saving $500 a
month by renting instead of owning. When
you factor in maintenance, insurance,
property taxes, and PMI, that's $6,000 a
year. You invest that, too. After 30
years, that stream of investments turns
into an additional $1.1 million.
claim_audit.assessment: [INDEPENDENT_CALCULATION_VERIFIED] $500/month at 10%/12 for 30 years = $1,130,244 (verified; annual end-of-year deposits would be $986,964). $872,470 + $1,130,244 = $2.0M. The $500/month renting saving contradicts the $2,000/month gap used earlier in the same video.
claim_audit.date_scope: Video publication context 2026-01-23; source dates and access limitations in companion receipts

claim_audit.claim: their house might be worth $1.2 2 million after 30 years of appreciation. Sounds good until you realize they paid $595,000 in interest alone on their mortgage.
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
their house might be worth $1.2 2
million after 30 years of appreciation.
Sounds good until you realize they paid
$595,000
in interest alone on their mortgage.
claim_audit.assessment: [INDEPENDENT_CALCULATION_VERIFIED] $500,000 at 3% for 30 years = $1,213,631 (verified). $595,000 interest matches a loan of about $425,000 at 7% ($592,913); the loan size is not stated. $150,000 maintenance (1% of $500,000 flat) and $180,000 property tax ($6,000 a year) are internally consistent. "Profit maybe $275,000" and the $4,367 payment cannot be reproduced from stated inputs (P&I on $425,000 is $2,828). The "factor of seven" ($2M / $275,000 = 7.3) inherits those unreproducible inputs.
claim_audit.date_scope: Video publication context 2026-01-23; source dates and access limitations in companion receipts

claim_audit.claim: people who bought houses when they cost two times annual income instead of six times did fine.
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
people who bought houses
when they cost two times annual income
instead of six times did fine.
claim_audit.assessment: [PRIMARY_SOURCE_DIRECTLY_INSPECTED] FRED MSPUS median sales price / MEHOINUSA646N median household income: 1995 $130,000 / $34,080 = 3.8x; 2005 4.9-5.0x; 2024 $426,800 / $83,160 = 5.1x; Q4 2025 $412,300 / 2024 income = 5.0x. Direction (affordability worsened) is supported nationally, but 2x and 6x are not; 6x may hold in expensive metros only. Price-to-income is not a measure of mortgage affordability, which also depends on the rate.
claim_audit.date_scope: Video publication context 2026-01-23; source dates and access limitations in companion receipts
